blocks.text: **Devmaxx topic:** Search. **Goal:** build a search system that is fast, relevant, and rebuildable.

rows: Fast on inverted index, even for fuzzy/prefix

blocks.text: **The core design decision: the search index is a *derived* structure.** It's built from the source of truth via CDC or an outbox relay. It can lag (seconds), and it can be rebuilt from scratch.
The structure behind every search engine.
**Forward index**: document → terms.

blocks.code:
Doc 1: "the quick brown fox"
Doc 2: "the lazy dog"

blocks.text: **Inverted index**: term → documents (with positions and frequencies).
**Query execution:**

items.text: `brown AND fox` → intersect the posting lists → Doc 1.
`brown OR fox`  → union.
`NOT brown`    → complement.

blocks.text: **The killer optimization: posting list compression + skipping.**

items.text: **Term dictionary** (FST in Lucene) maps terms to their posting lists.
**Block-based encoding** (e.g. Block-WAND / MaxScore): posting lists are split into blocks with

blocks.text: per-block statistics (max frequency, doc count), so the engine can **skip whole blocks** that can't affect the top-K. This is why phrase and proximity queries stay fast.
**Tokens vs. terms:** the analyzer (tokenizer + filters) turns raw text into terms:

items.text: Lowercase, stem (`running` → `run`), remove stop words, synonyms, n-grams, phonetic (Soundex,

blocks.text: Metaphone), language-specific (ICU), CJK bigrams.
BM25 (the default for lexical search)

blocks.code:
score(D, Q) = Σ_{t in Q} IDF(t) × (f(t,D) × (k1 + 1))
                      / (f(t,D) + k1 × (1 - b + b × |D|/avgdl))

items.text: `IDF(t)` — inverse document frequency: rare terms matter more.
`f(t,D)` — term frequency in the doc.
`k1` (~1.2) — term frequency saturation.
`b` (~0.75) — length normalization (longer docs don't win just by being long).

blocks.text: Other signals

rows: A match in the title counts more than in the body
Newer content ranks higher (huge for news, feeds)
A trained model over these features

blocks.text: Hybrid search
Combine lexical (BM25) and semantic (vector) retrieval:

Lexical is great at exact terms, IDs, error codes, and names; vector is great at concepts ("how do I stop my bill from charging twice" matching "cancel subscription"). Hybrid is now the default in production.
**Reranking**: retrieve broadly (e.g. 1000 candidates) with BM25 + vectors, then rerank the top 100 with a precise model (cross-encoder) — the standard modern pipeline:

blocks.code:
BM25 (1000) ──┐
              ├──► RRF merge ──► Reranker (cross-encoder) ──► Top 10
Vector (1000)─┘

blocks.text: **Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)** merges the two ranked lists without needing score calibration: `score(d) = Σ 1/(k + rank_i(d))` with k ≈ 60.

items.text: **Shingles** (n-grams) — index bigrams/trigrams of terms; a misspelled word still shares n-grams

blocks.text: exact and fast.
**Lucene (an inverted index) vs. Elasticsearch (a distributed layer on Lucene) vs. alternatives.**
5.1 Shard strategy

rows: Even distribution; no range queries across shards
Route by tenant/user so all docs for a tenant land on one shard

blocks.text: **Custom routing** is the most common pattern: `index_name_tenant_id` → all of a tenant's documents in one shard. Benefits: queries for one tenant hit one shard, and tenant deletion is a shard drop.
5.2 Replicas and search

items.text: Read replicas serve queries; the primary handles indexing.
If the primary falls behind, search results go stale (documented, monitored).
Near-real-time (NRT) indexing: a refresh interval (1s default) — a document isn't searchable

blocks.text: until the next refresh. This is the "index lag" users ask about.
5.3 Other engines

rows: General full-text + faceting, rich aggregations, widely used
Large scale, custom ranking at serving time, ML ranking, structured + unstructured
Fast, typo-tolerant, simple, good UX for e-commerce/ autocomplete
Developer-friendly, instant search, great for small-to-mid corpora
Simple, transactional, fine up to a few million docs

blocks.text: **Rule:** don't add a search engine until Postgres full-text stops being enough — usually around 1–10M documents or when you need typo tolerance, faceting, or relevance tuning.
Approach A: dual write (bad)

blocks.code:
App → DB write
App → ES write    ← if this fails, the index is out of sync

blocks.text: Approach B: CDC / outbox (correct)

blocks.code:
App → DB write + outbox row (one transaction)
Relay → reads outbox → indexes into ES

items.text: Reliable; at-least-once → the indexer is idempotent (document ID = primary key → an upsert).
Lag is measurable (outbox age) → alertable.
**Rebuild is always possible**: drop the index and replay from the DB.

blocks.text: Approach C: periodic full reindex (simple, for small data)

items.text: Export everything to a new index, then atomically swap the alias.
Downtime: none (alias swap), but the export is expensive and the DB is loaded.

blocks.text: **The alias swap is the key technique:**

blocks.code:
1. Create index `products_v2`
2. Index all documents
3. Verify count + spot checks
4. Atomically swap the alias: `products` → `products_v2`
5. Delete `products_v1`

blocks.text: Schema mapping decisions

items.text: **Dynamic mapping** is convenient but can cause **mapping explosion** (one field per random key

blocks.text: → thousands of fields → the cluster dies). Use explicit mappings or `dynamic: strict`.

items.text: Choose the right field type: `text` (analyzed) vs `keyword` (exact). A `text` field with a

blocks.text: `.keyword` sub-field gives both.

items.text: **Doc values** for sorting, aggregation, and scripting (columnar, on disk) — much faster than

blocks.text: `_source` scans.

items.text: `_source` stores the original JSON (needed for reindexing and returns) — enable it unless disk

blocks.text: pressure is severe.

items.text: **Disable `_source` + use `doc_values` only** for extreme scale, at the cost of reindexing pain.
**Analyzers**: define custom ones for code, product names (edge n-grams), and synonyms.

blocks.text: Facets are "category counts with filters" — the core of e-commerce search.

**Implementation:** for each facet field, keep a **doc-values column** of the term. Aggregation = scan the column, count. For high-cardinality fields this is expensive — use **global ordinals** and **eager global aggregations** (precompute counts per shard and merge) to avoid coordinating on every query.

**Important:** apply the filters for *other* facets before aggregating the current one — that's what makes the counts correct ("Apple: 320" should reflect the current category and price filters, not the total).

**Performance:** aggregations are the expensive part of a search query. Limit: `size` (top N buckets), use `terms` aggregation with `shard_size`, and consider `global` aggregations for constant facets.

blocks.text: **Design decisions:**

items.text: The search service is a **thin layer** over the search cluster that handles: user context,

items.text: **Multi-tenant**: one index per tenant (isolation, easy deletion) vs. one shared index with a

blocks.text: filter (cheaper, but a bad query can affect everyone and deletes are harder). Use routing-based routing for large tenants, a shared index for small ones.

blocks.text: `tenant_id`), never post-filter. Post-filtering breaks facet counts and pagination.

blocks.text: **`search_after` + Point in Time (PIT)** is the correct deep-pagination technique: open a PIT snapshot, then page with `search_after` using the last hit's sort values. Stable *and* fast.

items.text: **Build a mini inverted index.** Tokenize a small corpus, build the term→postings map, and implement AND / OR / phrase queries with positions. Verify the phrase query matches "quick brown fox" but not "brown quick fox".
**Implement BM25.** Score a query against your corpus and check that a rare term (high IDF) outranks a common term (like "the") for the same frequency.
**Build an autocomplete trie.** Given a prefix, return matching terms ranked by frequency. Measure the latency for 3-, 5-, and 8-character prefixes.
**Spelling correction with a delete index.** Generate all deletes at distance ≤2 for a vocabulary, build the index, and correct "recieve" → "receive". Compare with brute-force Levenshtein on speed.

**Shard a search index.** Take 1M documents, split them across 3 shards with a hash function, and implement a coordinating query that fans out and merges. Compare latency against a single-shard query. Then add a term-based aggregation across shards and check the counts.
**CDC indexer.** Write to Postgres + an outbox; a relay indexes into a search store (Elasticsearch or Whoosh). Kill the relay mid-flight and verify the index catches up with no duplicates.

blocks.text: Good: "I'd use Elasticsearch for full-text and facets, with the DB as the source of truth and an outbox relay indexing changes, so the index can lag a second but is always rebuildable. I'd shard by tenant ID so tenant queries hit one shard. Ranking is BM25 with title boosting, plus recency decay."

Better: "For semantic matching I'll do hybrid search — BM25 for exact terms and vector search for concepts — merged with RRF and reranked by a cross-encoder. I'll use a PIT + search_after for pagination, and I'll log every query with the results and clicks so I can tune synonyms and detect zero-result queries."
Red flags: indexing directly from the request path (double-write); treating the search index as the source of truth; no plan for zero-result queries; no relevance evaluation.

selfCheck.q: **What is an inverted index, and what does it enable that a forward index can't do fast?**
selfCheck.a: A map from term → list of documents (with positions/frequencies). It makes "which documents contain this term" a direct lookup instead of a scan, enabling fast full-text matching, scoring, phrase/proximity queries, and aggregations.

selfCheck.q: **What does the analyzer do, and name three filters?**
selfCheck.a: It tokenizes text and normalizes the tokens: lowercasing, stemming ("running"→"run"), removing stop words, applying synonyms, generating n-grams, and phonetic normalization.

selfCheck.q: **Explain BM25's IDF term and why it matters.**
selfCheck.a: IDF = log(total docs / docs containing the term). It makes rare, discriminative terms count far more than ubiquitous ones ("the" contributes almost nothing; a specific product name dominates the score). Without it, every document scores highly on common terms.

selfCheck.q: **What are the two signals BM25 doesn't capture that matter in real search?**
selfCheck.a: **Recency/time decay** (critical for news, feeds, job listings) and **personalization /popularity / business signals** (click-through, stock, margin). BM25 only knows about text.

selfCheck.q: **What is hybrid search and how do you merge two differently-scaled score lists?**
selfCheck.a: Lexical (BM25) plus semantic (vector) retrieval. Their scores aren't on the same scale, so merge by **rank** rather than score — typically Reciprocal Rank Fusion: `score(d) = Σ 1/(k + rank_i(d))`.

selfCheck.q: **What is a cross-encoder reranker and why do you rerank only the top 100?**
selfCheck.a: A model that reads the query and document *together* (unlike bi-encoder vectors) for accurate scoring — much slower, so you only run it on the top ~100 candidates from cheap retrieval.

selfCheck.q: **How does an FST make autocomplete fast?**
selfCheck.a: A finite state transducer shares the common prefixes of terms in a compact automaton, so a prefix lookup is O(length of prefix) with a small memory footprint — versus scanning a sorted list or a hash map.

selfCheck.q: **How does a delete index (SymSpell) enable spell correction?**
selfCheck.a: Precompute, for each vocabulary term, all strings within edit distance 1–2 (its "deletes"). A misspelling is, by definition, a delete-or-two away from the correct word, so an exact lookup in the delete index finds the candidate instantly — much faster than scanning the vocabulary computing Levenshtein distances.

selfCheck.q: **What is `s-maxage`... no — what is the difference between shard and replica in a search cluster?**
selfCheck.a: A **shard** is a slice of the index (part of the data) that can be searched independently and is the unit of parallelism and storage. A **replica** is a copy of a shard for availability and read throughput. Searches fan out across shards and merge; reads can be served from replicas.

selfCheck.q: **Why is custom routing by tenant ID the most common sharding strategy?**
selfCheck.a: All of a tenant's documents land in one shard → single-shard queries (fast, no fan-out), simple tenant deletion (drop the shard/index), and no cross-tenant leakage. It's how most multi-tenant search systems are built.

selfCheck.q: **What is mapping explosion and how do you prevent it?**
selfCheck.a: When dynamic mapping creates a new field for every document (e.g. a map/dictionary field with random keys), the cluster accumulates thousands of fields and dies. Prevent with explicit mappings or `dynamic: strict`/`false`, and by using `nested`/`flattened` for arbitrary keys.

selfCheck.q: **Why is dual-write indexing to a search engine dangerous?**
selfCheck.a: Because the DB write and the index write are separate operations: if the index write fails, the document is missing from search with no record of the failure, and it silently drifts. Fix with CDC/outbox (reliable, at-least-once, idempotent) and periodic full reindex.

selfCheck.q: **How do you reindex a large corpus without downtime?**
selfCheck.a: Index into a **new index** (in parallel, using `slices` + `search_after`), verify counts and spot checks, then **atomically swap the alias** to point at the new index, then delete the old one. No downtime, instant rollback.

selfCheck.q: **Why is deep pagination (`from: 100000`) a problem, and what's the fix?**
selfCheck.a: `from + size` requires the engine to collect and rank all `from+size` matching documents —O(n) memory and time, and it gets worse with each page. Fix: `search_after` with the last hit's sort values, ideally inside a Point in Time (PIT) for a consistent snapshot.

selfCheck.q: **Why must authorization filters be applied inside the search query rather than after?**
selfCheck.a: Because post-filtering removes non-matching documents *after* the engine computed the top-K, so you get fewer than `size` results and, crucially, **facet counts and pagination are computed over the unfiltered set** — wrong counts and short pages. Filtering must be part of the query.

selfCheck.q: **What is NRT indexing, and what's the user-visible implication?**
selfCheck.a: "Near real time" — the index refreshes periodically (1s by default), so a newly created document isn't searchable until the next refresh. Users who create and immediately search see stale results; the fix is either a shorter refresh interval (costly) or "search as you type" that queries the primary directly for the newest items.

selfCheck.q: **How do you make facet counts respect the other active filters?**
selfCheck.a: Apply the *other* active filters to the query first, then aggregate the current facet over the filtered result set. In Elasticsearch this means a `post_filter` for the current facet and including the others in the `query`/`filter` clause — a subtle but critical distinction.

selfCheck.q: **What are "zero-result queries" and how do you use them?**
selfCheck.a: Queries that return no results — a huge signal of user intent failure (typos, wrong vocabulary, missing content). Use them to build synonym lists, "did you mean" suggestions, and to identify content gaps worth creating.

selfCheck.q: **When is Postgres full-text enough, and when do you need a dedicated engine?**
selfCheck.a: Postgres full-text (`tsvector` + GIN) is enough for a few million docs, simple tokenization, and when you need search to be transactional with the data. Move to Elasticsearch/Vespa/Typesense when you need typo tolerance, complex faceting, relevance tuning, per-field boosts, or scale beyond a few million documents.

selfCheck.q: **What is a hot shard in a search cluster and how do you fix it?**
selfCheck.a: One shard receives disproportionate traffic or holds disproportionate data (a huge tenant, a hot category). Fix: custom routing to distribute that tenant's docs across more shards, add replicas for read capacity, split the tenant into sub-tenants, or increase shard count and reindex.
